rationale: The concern is valid, and this stays partial. Provisioning and teardown are documented: the CKS API creates, lists, updates and deletes clusters, the Terraform provider manages CKS infrastructure, and the Cluster Autoscaler scales GPU Node Pools. Workloads can then run through kubectl via generated kubeconfigs or through SUNK. However, monitoring is only described as Grafana dashboards, and the MCP server's "supported changes" are unspecified, while Capacity Finder and quota viewing and increases are documented only in the Cloud Console, so a human is still in the loop. Missing for 10: documented programmatic GPU and Node Pool monitoring via API, CLI or MCP; API or CLI capacity discovery and quota handling without the Console; explicit MCP provisioning or teardown capability; hands-on corroboration of an unattended end-to-end flow.

A live probe returned HTTP 200 for https://docs.coreweave.com/llms.txt, which serves a structured markdown index titled 'CoreWeave Docs'. The docs pages themselves are published as .md URLs (e.g. cks.md, terraform.md), so an agent can be pointed directly at machine-readable documentation. missing for 10: first-party documentation describing or promoting the llms.txt / agent-oriented docs, evidence of full-content variants (e.g. llms-full.txt) or index completeness, and independent corroboration of agents using it.

The only on-topic evidence is a one-line docs mention of a first-party Mission Control Agent for investigating the customer's environment and making supported changes. That plausibly delivers AI-generated analysis of the user's own infrastructure inside the product, but its depth is undocumented. Billing insights and Grafana dashboards are conventional reporting, not AI-generated, so they earn no credit. Missing for 10: detailed docs on what insights or suggestions the agent produces and from which data (telemetry, logs, usage, cost), how it surfaces them in the Cloud Console, and any independent or hands-on corroboration.

CoreWeave offers infrastructure-level automation that runs unattended. The Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler scales Node Pools on its own as workload demand changes, bucket lifecycle policies expire objects automatically, and Slurm via SUNK runs batch jobs in the background. Terraform and the APIs allow programmatic orchestration, but you must assemble the automations yourself from Kubernetes and Slurm primitives rather than through a first-class automation feature. Missing for 10: a native scheduled-task or trigger system, agent-driven automation workflows, documentation on setting up autonomous background automations end to end, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Bearer API access tokens plus downloadable kubeconfigs let kubectl run without the Cloud Console.
